title: Deep in-the-money calls rebalance themselves through delta
summary: The speaker buys deep in-the-money calls as stock replacement and never rolls the strike. After a rally, the option's leverage falls, which works like selling into strength. After a drop, delta falls so dollar losses slow, while leverage on the remaining capital rises, which works like buying the dip.

steps.caption: The stock trades at $100. We own a one-year $75 call, deep in the money, as a stock replacement.
The $75 strike is fixed. The speaker never rolls it, whatever the stock does.
Delta is near 0.90 at $100. If the stock rallies, delta moves toward 1.0 while the call's leverage shrinks: like trimming into strength.
If the stock falls toward the strike, delta drops. Each further dollar down costs less: like a built-in brake.
Gamma shows how fast delta changes. It peaks near the strike, where the elasticity is largest.
Theta is small for a deep in-the-money LEAPS call, so the carrying cost is low.

takeaways: Do not roll deep in-the-money call strikes after a rally; the falling leverage acts like selling into strength.
After a drop, the lower delta slows dollar losses and the leverage on remaining capital rises, like adding on weakness.
The speaker calls this delta elasticity and lets it work instead of trading.
caveats: The 'buy the dip, sell the rip' effect is a change in exposure, not actual trades. Total loss of the premium is still possible.
The transcript is cut off before the speaker's bottom line.

scenario.label: 2018-2024: two bear markets and two rallies

backtest.note: One-year 90-delta call held without strike rolls; replaced 90 days before expiry.
